ch09.title: Bread for Five Thousand
ch09.b001: A Story from the Old Boat
ch09.b002: Even after they came back from Nazareth, something had not quite left the Master’s face. He laughed as brightly as ever, but beneath the laughter lay a thin layer of unfamiliar sadness. The apostles all noticed it, and none of them spoke of it. Andrew could guess where it came from. A man dragged to the edge of a cliff by the people of his own town does not shake that off overnight. Andrew did not know what one ought to do at such a time. He had grown up the eldest, and he had always been good at shouldering other people’s loads; but words that might ease another man’s sorrow had never come easily to him. So he saw to the work instead—where the evangelists would sleep, which houses the women would visit, whose turn it was to go fishing. Work was easier than words.
ch09.b003: Then came a Sunday morning. The talk the night before had gone on very late, and few of the company in Zebedee’s house were up for breakfast. When Andrew went down to the shore he found the Master sitting alone in the old fishing boat that belonged to him and Peter, the boat they always kept free for the Master’s use. Every seam had been daubed and daubed again with pitch, and in the stern there was a raised seat that was good for sitting. Andrew did not go nearer. He could see the Master was deep in thought. But the solitude did not last long. People began to drift in from Capernaum and the villages nearby, and by ten o’clock nearly a thousand of them crowded the water’s edge, calling out for him.
ch09.b004: Peter came down to the boat and asked whether he should speak to them. No, the Master said; this time he would tell them a story. And sitting on the raised seat, he began to speak to the crowd along the shore. A sower went out to sow. Some of the seed fell along the path, where it was trampled and the birds ate it. Some fell on rocky ground with little soil; it sprang up quickly, but when the sun rose it withered, having no root. Some fell among thorns and was choked. But the seed that fell on good ground bore thirtyfold, sixtyfold, a hundredfold. And whoever had ears to hear, he said, let him hear.
ch09.b005: A murmur ran along the shore. That was all. It was not a sermon, not an exposition of the law; it was a farmer’s tale. Andrew saw puzzled faces among the crowd, heads tilted to one side. The apostles’ faces looked no different. That evening in Zebedee’s garden Matthew asked on behalf of them all why the Master spoke such dark sayings to people who were seeking the truth. The Master answered that he had taught them patiently all this time. To them it was given to know the mysteries of the kingdom; but from now on, to the undiscerning crowds and to those who sought to destroy him, he would speak in parables. Those who truly wanted to enter would search out the meaning. Those who listened only to lay a trap would see without seeing and hear without hearing.
ch09.b006: The apostles did not fully understand that either. Andrew and Thomas stayed behind to go on talking with the Master, while Peter and the others drew off to another part of the garden and put their heads together. Over his shoulder Andrew could hear his brother’s voice: loud, fast, full of certainty. When that voice climbed so high, Andrew could usually tell what was about to happen.
ch09.b008: Peter and his group decided that the parable was a kind of picture puzzle in which every piece had a hidden meaning. Peter came to the Master and asked him to explain it. The Master said he wished to hold nothing back from him, but first Peter should tell him how he had interpreted it. Peter hesitated for a moment, then laid it all out without a stumble. The sower was the preacher, the seed was the word of God, the birds were Satan, the rocky ground stood for those whose fervor was only skin-deep, the thorns were the cares of the world and the lure of riches. It sounded convincing. As a younger brother he had never been short of fluency.
ch09.b009: When the Master asked whether anyone else had something to offer, Nathaniel stood up. He politely granted that there was much that was good in Peter’s reading, then said he saw it a little differently. The seed was the gospel of the kingdom, the sowers were the messengers of the kingdom, and the birds were not Satan but a man’s habits of life and the desires of the flesh. The thorns were less about riches than about pride and jealousy and envy. When Nathaniel finished, the garden split in two. Peter’s side and Nathaniel’s side were almost even. Voices rose. Peter and Nathaniel went off into the house altogether, each bent on talking the other round.
ch09.b010: Andrew stood at one side of the garden and watched. An hour ago they had all been one group that had heard one story. Now they were two factions. He looked at the Master. The Master did not stop them. He let the confusion run to its fullest pitch. Then he clapped his hands. When they had all gathered around him again, he asked whether anyone had anything to say before he spoke.
ch09.b011: After a moment’s silence Thomas spoke up. He remembered, he said, something the Master had once told them: when they used illustrations in their preaching they should use true stories rather than fables, choose a story that fitted the one central truth they meant to teach, and not try to hang a spiritual meaning on every small detail of it. In his view, Peter and Nathaniel were both wrong. And the proof was that an hour ago they had all been of one mind, and now they were split into two camps and in danger of missing the very truth the Master had meant to convey.
ch09.b012: The garden grew quiet. Then Andrew stood up. In a voice clearer than he himself expected, he said he was persuaded that Thomas was right, and that he would like to hear how Thomas understood the parable. It was not often that Andrew declared another man to be right. It was not praise; it was a verdict. Yet Thomas glanced at him once, and in that look was the surprise of a man who has been handed something.
ch09.b013: At the Master’s nod, Thomas spoke briefly. The parable taught one great truth, he said. However faithfully they preached the gospel, the results would differ, and those differences would come from conditions they had little or no power to control. Most of his fellows were ready to agree, and even Peter and Nathaniel were on their way over to speak with him, when the Master rose. Well done, Thomas, he said; you have grasped what parables are for. And he added that Peter and Nathaniel had done them all equal good, for they had shown so plainly the danger of turning his parables into allegories. Such flights of imagination might be profitable enough in one’s own heart, he said, but it was a mistake to offer them as public teaching.
ch09.b014: With the tension gone, Peter and Nathaniel complimented each other on their interpretations. Peter clapped Nathaniel on the shoulder and laughed, and Nathaniel said that turning the birds into Satan had been a bit unfair to the birds. That night, before they went to bed, every one of the apostles except the Alpheus twins tried his own hand at interpreting the parable. Even Judas Iscariot came up with a quite plausible one. Andrew listened to all of it, and then his eyes met his brother’s. Today his brother had been wrong. And yet, wrong as he was, he could laugh like that, wide open. Andrew envied him that. He wanted to tell his brother that his reading had not been bad either. Once again the words stopped somewhere in his throat.
ch09.b015: All that week the Master taught from the boat in parables: the enemy who sowed weeds among the wheat, and the householder who let both grow together until harvest; the mustard seed, smallest of seeds, that grew into a tree where the birds came to rest; the leaven hidden in three measures of meal until all of it rose; the treasure hidden in a field, and the merchant who sold everything for one pearl of great price; the net that drew up every kind of fish. And each evening he explained their meaning more fully to the apostles and the evangelists.
ch09.b017: The crowds grew larger every day. On the Sabbath the Master slipped away into the hills, but by Sunday morning the people were back. That day, early in the afternoon, after Peter had preached and the Master had spoken to the multitude, he turned to the apostles and said he was weary of the throngs; let them cross to the other side and rest for a day. Simon Zelotes heard those words with a strange feeling. Weary. He had never once thought of this man as someone who could grow tired. Three boats carrying young evangelists followed behind.
ch09.b018: Toward evening a cold wind came pouring down from the western gorges. The Sea of Galilee lies some seven hundred feet below the level of the sea, and the air that warms over it during the day tends, after sunset, to be overrun all at once by the cool air rushing down from the ravines. Such gales come suddenly and can leave as suddenly. This one was among the worst those fishermen had ever known. Before they could furl the sail, the wind tore it away. Waves began to break over the side. Now they had only their oars, and they pulled for the shore, a little more than a mile and a half off.
ch09.b019: Simon Zelotes took an oar as well. He was no fisherman. Within minutes the skin was gone from his palms, and spray drove into his mouth and nose. Beside him one of the twins gritted his teeth and pulled in a steady rhythm, and Simon matched it. There was no room for thinking. Each time the boat lifted and dropped, his stomach turned over. In the middle of it all he looked toward the stern. Under a small shelter there, the Master lay asleep. The boat was being tossed like a toy, and still he did not wake.
ch09.b020: As water rose in the bottom of the boat, Peter, who had the right-hand oar near the stern, let go of it, ran to the Master, and shook him awake. Did he not know they were in a terrible storm? If he did not save them, they would all perish. The Master came out into the rain. He looked first at Peter, then peered through the dark at the men straining at the oars, then looked at Peter again. Why were they all so full of fear, he asked; where was their faith? Peace, he said; be quiet. Hardly were the words spoken when the wind died. The waves lay down; the clouds, having spent themselves in a short shower, broke apart; and the stars came out overhead.
ch09.b021: Simon Zelotes sat gripping his oar and stared up at that sky. His heart was still pounding like a drum. The wind had obeyed a single word. That was what he believed. The other apostles believed it too, and for the rest of his life Peter never tired of telling how even the winds and the waves obeyed him. Later the Master told them plainly that he had spoken not to the wind but to their frightened hearts. It made no difference. As far as those who set down this record can judge, the calm that night was simply a matter of timing. But to Simon, that night, it could not have been anything else. If this man could still the wind, what was a Roman legion? He opened and closed his raw hands. They hurt. And he was glad.
ch09.b022: The night was so calm and beautiful that they slept in the boats and went ashore only after sunrise. They had landed near the village of Kheresa on the eastern shore. The steep hillside was honeycombed with caves cut into the rock, many of them ancient tombs. As they passed the burying ground, a man came rushing out of the caverns at them. His name was Amos. In a lucid interval he had once come over to Bethsaida, heard the preaching, and become a halfhearted believer; but whenever his affliction came back he fled to the tombs and howled there. Now he fell at the Master’s feet and begged him not to torment him, for he was possessed by many devils. The Master looked down at the man crouched there like an animal, then took him by the hand and raised him up. Amos was not possessed by any devil, he told him; he had already heard the good news that he was a son of God. And he bade him come out of this spell. The light came back into Amos’s eyes. He sat right there and talked with the apostles in his right mind.
ch09.b023: While the swineherds ran off to the village with the news, dogs set upon a small, untended herd of about thirty swine and drove most of them over the cliff into the sea. The villagers believed the devils the Master had cast out of Amos had gone into the swine. Amos believed it. Every one of the apostles except Thomas believed it. So did Simon Zelotes. Early the next morning the gentile swine-keepers sent a delegation to Peter and Andrew asking them to go and take their prophet with them. They knew he was a holy man, they said, but the gods of their country did not know him, and they were afraid of losing more swine. The Master told Andrew they would go back to their own place. Amos pleaded to come with them, but the Master would not allow it. He was to go home to his own people, Jesus said, and show them what great things God had done for him.
ch09.b025: When their boat came back on Tuesday forenoon, the story of Amos had already reached Bethsaida and Capernaum. Out of the crowd waiting on the shore, Jairus, one of the rulers of the synagogue, pushed his way forward and fell at the Master’s feet. His little daughter, his only child, was dying. The Master said he would go with him. In a narrow street, with the crowd jostling him on every side, the Master suddenly stopped and said that someone had touched him. Peter asked what he could mean, with the crowd pressing on them like this. The Master said he had felt living energy go out from him. A woman came forward and knelt—Veronica, from Caesarea-Philippi. For years she had suffered from bleeding and had spent all she had on physicians; she had believed that if she could only touch the hem of his garment she would be well. The Master raised her up and told her, daughter, your faith has made you whole. Not the hem of a garment, but faith.
ch09.b026: Before they reached Jairus’s house a servant came out to say that the girl was dead. The Master took only Peter, James, and John in with him. Philip stayed in the yard with the others and listened to the din of the flute players and the mourners. After a while the noise stopped, and from inside the house came the sound of a child’s feet crossing a room. The Master told them to give her something to eat. Then he gathered the family and explained that the girl had been in a coma after a long fever, and that he had only roused her, not raised her from the dead. He explained the same thing to the apostles. But every one of them believed he had brought her back from death. So did Philip. He was a man who believed what he could see, and what he had heard in that yard was the sound of wailing stopping.
ch09.b027: As they came away from the house, two blind men led by a dumb boy followed them, crying out to be healed. The Master’s fame as a healer was then at its very height. Wherever he went, the sick and afflicted were waiting. Philip looked at the Master’s face. There were dark shadows under his eyes. His step was heavier than before. His friends began to fear he would go on until he actually collapsed. Philip thought about what he could do as steward: better bread, a quieter place to sleep. But it was not bread this man was short of.
ch09.b029: On Friday the Master declared a week’s furlough so that everyone could go home before getting ready to go up to Jerusalem for the Passover. But more than half of the disciples refused to leave him, and the crowd grew larger by the day. So on Sunday morning, March 27, leaving some of the evangelists to talk to the multitude, the Master and the twelve slipped away by boat to a beautiful park south of Bethsaida-Julias, a favorite resort of the people of Capernaum.
ch09.b030: Before they left, Philip packed three days’ food for the thirteen of them: barley loaves, dried fish, a few figs. The lad Mark, their boy of all chores, was put in charge of it. Every time Philip looked at that bag, he felt at ease. Three days. The reckoning was exact. But the people had seen which way the boat was heading. They hired every craft they could find and came after them, and those who could not get a boat walked around the upper end of the lake. By late afternoon more than a thousand had gathered. By Monday afternoon there were more than three thousand. By Wednesday noon some five thousand men, women, and children were in the park. The weather was fine; the rainy season was nearly over.
ch09.b031: All through those three days Philip never stopped reckoning. When would the food the people had brought run out? How much bread could be bought in the nearest villages? By the afternoon of the third day, about half of the crowd had nothing left. There was no tented city of David Zebedee’s here. And Philip had made no provision for a multitude of this size either. Still the people would not leave. Philip knew why. Something stronger than hunger was holding them there.
ch09.b032: A whisper was going around. The Master had chosen this quiet spot on purpose, it said, to stay clear of Herod and of Jerusalem, out of the reach of all his enemies. Here he meant to be made king. The ringleader was a young evangelist named Joab. The excitement of the crowd rose by the hour. The apostles themselves were divided. Peter, John, Simon Zelotes, and Judas Iscariot wanted it. Andrew, James, Nathaniel, and Thomas were against it. Matthew, the twins, and Philip took no side. Philip knew nothing about politics. He knew only the number five thousand. And he knew how small his bag was before that number.
ch09.b033: About five o’clock on Wednesday afternoon the Master sent James Alpheus to call Andrew and Philip. What should they do with this multitude? he asked. The people had been with them three days, and many of them were hungry; they had nothing to eat. Philip and Andrew exchanged a look. Philip spoke first: the Master should send the people away so they could buy food in the villages round about. Andrew, who feared the king plot would come to a head, quickly agreed—let the crowd go, and let the Master get some rest. By now others of the twelve had come up. The Master said he did not want to send them away hungry. Could the apostles not feed them?
ch09.b034: That was too much for Philip, and he said so at once. Where in this countryside could they buy bread? Two hundred denarii worth would not give each of them a mouthful. It was not a complaint; it was an honest reckoning, and Philip had seldom in his life reckoned wrong. The Master said the people were like sheep without a shepherd and that he wanted to feed them; what did they have with them? While Philip went to work out the sums with Matthew and Judas, Andrew went to find the lad Mark. He came back and said there were only five barley loaves and two dried fishes. And Peter promptly added that they themselves had not yet eaten that evening.
ch09.b035: For those few minutes Philip stood close beside Matthew and Judas, working it out. Judas cupped the purse at his belt in his palm as though weighing it.
ch09.b036: “Empty it all and it still won’t come to two hundred,” he said. “And there’s no bread for sale anywhere near here.”
ch09.b037: Matthew said nothing. He was thinking of what remained in the chest at his own house. But even if he brought every coin of it here, what would there be to buy? Philip looked from one face to the other. Three men who knew how to count had come together and reached the same answer: it cannot be done. All three were honest, and all three were right. Philip was not ashamed to take that answer to the Master. Only, strangely, his heart felt heavy. He had never known before that an honest sum could be so lonely.
ch09.b038: For a while the Master said nothing. There was a faraway look in his eyes. No one spoke. Long afterward, Philip still could not have said how long that silence lasted. At last the Master turned to Andrew and told him to bring the loaves and fishes. When Andrew held out the basket, the Master told them to have the people sit down on the grass in companies of a hundred and to put a leader over each company. And they were to bring all the evangelists to him.
ch09.b040: Philip ran through the crowd seating people by hundreds. This was something he was good at. The twins helped, and between them they sat the people in rows as neatly as if they were pegging tents. The grass was still green. The sun was sinking toward the western hills. When the five thousand were seated on the grass, the hum of voices died away. Philip turned, out of breath. And then he saw.
ch09.b041: The Master took the loaves in his hands and gave thanks. Then he broke them and gave them to the apostles. The apostles passed them to their associates, and their associates carried them out to the crowd. Bread was put into Philip’s hands. He passed it to the man beside him and took more. Passed it on and took more again. His hands kept trying to count. Five loaves. How many pieces had they been broken into? How many people had they reached? But the sums would not come out. No—there was no place for a sum to stand. The bread did not run out of his hands. The fish went round the same way. At some moment, Philip stopped counting. It was the first time in his life.
ch09.b042: He had always been the one who wanted to be shown. Even in the middle of the Master’s deepest discourses he would break in and ask to be shown. The Master had never once rebuked him for it. Today he had not asked to be shown anything. And yet he saw. The bag he had packed, his reckoning of three days, his reckoning of two hundred denarii—all those honest sums were quietly overflowing in his hands. Philip’s throat tightened. It was not only astonishment. It was the generosity of it. In this man he had never once seen anything small or grudging, and today that generosity filled the stomachs of five thousand and still had more to spare. He knelt on the grass and handed a fish to a child. The child took it and laughed. Philip laughed too. Tears ran down into his beard.
ch09.b043: They all ate and were filled. Then the Master told them to gather up the broken pieces that were left, so that nothing would be lost. Philip understood that better than anyone. They were a steward’s words. The fragments they gathered filled twelve baskets. Philip stood holding one of them in his arms. It was heavy. This was the first and only nature miracle the Master ever performed by his own deliberate intention. His followers called many things miracles that were not, but this one was truly supernatural.
ch09.b045: Simon Zelotes stood in the middle of the well-fed crowd and felt the air change. It was like the stillness just before the wind rises. These people had been taught from childhood that when the Messiah, the son of David, came, the land would flow again with milk and honey, and bread from heaven would fall as the manna had fallen on their fathers in the wilderness. And now that bread was in their mouths. The power to feed was the right to rule. Someone shouted. The shout spread. Five thousand people rose to their feet as one and cried out: make him king.
ch09.b046: The cry struck the nearby rocks and echoed back. Simon’s whole body prickled. In Zealot cellars, on mountain paths by night, he had dreamed of this sound more times than he could count. Without knowing it, he had raised his fist. Peter was shouting too. John’s eyes were shining. Simon saw Judas Iscariot turn toward the Master with a look that said: this time, this time, do not draw back. The man who stilled the wind has fed five thousand, Simon thought. Only one word is left to be spoken.
ch09.b047: Before the echo had died away, the Master stepped up onto a great stone and raised his right hand to quiet them. “My children,” he said. They meant well, he told them, but they were shortsighted and material-minded. There was a brief pause. Standing there in the glow of that eastern twilight, the strong Galilean looked every inch a king. Simon held his breath. They wanted to make him king, the Master said, not because their souls had been lit by a great truth but because their stomachs had been filled with bread. How often had he told them that his kingdom was not of this world? The kingdom of heaven was a spiritual brotherhood, and no man ruled it from a material throne. Now they should all go home. And if they must have a king, let the Father of lights be enthroned in each one’s heart.
ch09.b048: The words cut deeper than a sword. The crowd broke up, stunned and disheartened. Many who had believed in him turned back that day and followed him no more. Simon Zelotes stood there unable even to lower his fist. It had frozen in the air. The apostles stood speechless beside the twelve baskets. None of them spoke. Only the lad Mark said, as if to himself, that the Master had refused to be their king. The child’s voice carried far too clearly across the evening grass.
ch09.b049: Simon looked down at the baskets. They were full of broken bread. Here was the proof that heaven had opened. And the man who had opened it had just pushed away a crown. Simon could not understand it. Anger surged up in him, and then something deeper came after it. The Master’s calm. A face that had not wavered in the least while five thousand people shouted him king. The very thing Simon admired most in this man had broken his dream today. He could not hate that calm. That was what made it so hard to bear.
ch09.b050: Before going off alone into the hills, the Master turned to Andrew. He was to take his brethren back to Zebedee’s house and pray with them, the Master said—and especially for his brother, Simon Peter.
ch09.b052: The apostles got into the boat without their Master. It had never happened before. Never once had he sent them all off by themselves and refused to come with them. In silence they began to row west toward Bethsaida. Had he forsaken them? What did all this mean? No one asked aloud, but everyone was thinking it. Simon Zelotes bent his head over his oar. Judas Iscariot leaned on the gunwale and watched the eastern hills recede. Of all the twelve, none was so crushed and downcast as Peter.
ch09.b053: When darkness fell, a strong headwind rose against them, and they made almost no headway. As he rowed, Andrew watched his brother. Peter nodded over his oar and at last collapsed into sleep. Andrew and James laid him on the cushioned seat in the stern. Andrew brushed the wet hair off his brother’s face. Then he took up his oar again. With every stroke he prayed silently, as the Master had told him. For my brother. He had seen how loudly his brother had shouted at the foot of that rock today. And he had seen how his brother’s face had caved in when the shout was struck down. The higher a man climbs, the farther he falls. Andrew was afraid of how far his brother might fall.
ch09.b054: Peter dreamed. He dreamed that the Master came to them walking on the sea. When the Master seemed about to pass the boat by, Peter cried out in his sleep, Master, save us! Those near the stern heard him. In the dream the Master told them to take heart, it was he, they need not be afraid. And in the dream Peter asked, if it was truly the Master, to be allowed to come to him on the water. And he began to walk. Then the rough waves frightened him, and as he started to sink he cried out, Lord, save me! This time many of the twelve heard the cry. In the dream the Master stretched out his hand and pulled him up, asking him why he had doubted, he of little faith.
ch09.b055: And at that moment Peter really did get up and step over the side into the water. Andrew was the first to reach for him. James and John grabbed his clothing right behind. As the three of them hauled him out, Peter woke from his dream. He sat on the bottom of the boat, soaked through, gasping for breath. Andrew rubbed his brother’s wet back for a long time. He said nothing. There was nothing to say. All his life Peter believed the Master had truly come to them that night across the water. Andrew never tried to set him right. Whatever his brother had laid hold of that night, it had certainly brought him up out of the sea.
ch09.b056: Before dawn on Thursday they anchored offshore near Zebedee’s house and slept until nearly noon. Andrew was first up and went down to the shore. Two figures were sitting on a stone by the water: the Master and the lad Mark. Soon after midnight the two of them had set out on foot around the lake and across the river, back to Bethsaida, while many of the crowd and the young evangelists searched all night through the eastern hills for him. Andrew stopped. The Master looked round. His face was tired, but at peace. Andrew did not know what to say. So he simply went and sat down beside him. There was only the sound of the water lapping the stones. It was enough.
ch09.b058: Of the five thousand who had been fed, and who, with full stomachs and empty hearts, had wanted to make him king, only about five hundred kept on following him. Before they could hear that he was back, the Master had Andrew gather the twelve and their associates, the women included. How long must he bear with them? he asked. All these months he had taught them the truths of the kingdom, and still they were moved by material motives instead of spiritual ones. They had fed the multitude, but it had not made those people hunger for the bread of life. They had wanted to make him king so that they might have bread without toiling for it—and many of the apostles and disciples had played some part in it. Were there not enemies enough among the religious leaders without turning the civil rulers against them as well?
ch09.b059: Simon Zelotes listened with his head bowed. The rebuke was meant for him too. He knew that. But in one corner of his heart the twilight above that great stone was still burning. That day the man had truly looked like a king. Simon could not rub out the picture.
ch09.b060: Andrew, listening to the rebuke, watched his brother. Peter could not lift his head. Since they had pulled him from the sea, he had grown quiet. When a man whose words always ran ahead of him falls silent, it weighed on Andrew more than any shouting could. That evening Andrew sat beside his brother and the two of them mended a net together. They hardly spoke. Let the hands do their work while the heart rests: that was all an older brother could give a younger, and Andrew believed it was one shape that prayer could take.
ch09.b061: The Master said he wanted a few days’ rest and that no one was to follow. They went by boat to the region of Gennesaret and for two or three days rested and slept in the house of a wealthy believer. Every afternoon the Master sat with the twelve. They had become serious, sober, chastened men—men woken out of a dream. Yet their old ideas of the Messiah did not drain away overnight. In less than a month the open followers of Jesus, more than fifty thousand in Galilee alone, shrank to fewer than five hundred. The Master wanted them to learn for themselves how fickle the crowd’s acclaim could be. On the second night he told them the parable of the sower again. An appeal to men’s feelings was fleeting, he said, and an appeal to the intellect alone was barren; only an appeal to the spirit that lives within a man could bring lasting change. He also warned them that the religious rulers in Jerusalem would conspire with Herod Antipas to destroy them. The twelve began to see more deeply, though not yet completely, that he was not going to sit on David’s throne, and that the bread for five thousand and the cry to make him king had been the peak of the people’s craving for wonders. Dimly they foresaw that beyond it lay a time of sifting, a cruel time. And the Master told them that, even in feeding the five thousand, he had not yielded to his compassion until he had first made sure it was the Father’s will.
ch09.b062: On Sunday, April 3, the Master set out for Jerusalem with the twelve alone, going by way of Gerasa and Philadelphia to avoid the crowds. Again at this Passover he forbade them to teach. At Bethany the apostles split up two by two to stay in different homes; Simon Zelotes and Judas Iscariot lodged with friends in Jerusalem. In those weeks they felt on their own skin how bitter the feeling against the Master had grown. When they left Jerusalem on April 24, every one of them believed a crisis was close at hand. As soon as they reached Bethsaida on Friday, April 29, the Master sent Andrew to ask the ruler of the synagogue for leave to speak in the Capernaum synagogue at the next afternoon’s Sabbath service. The Master knew it would be the last time he would be allowed to speak there.
ch09.b064: The events follow Papers 151 and 152: Jesus’s sadness after Nazareth (151:0.2); the first telling of the parable of the sower from the boat and Matthew’s question (151:1.1–1.5); the interpretations of Peter and Nathaniel, Thomas’s words, Andrew’s support of Thomas, and the night when all tried their hand (151:2.1–2.8); the further parables (151:4.1–4.7); the storm on the lake (151:5.1–5.7); Amos of Kheresa and the swine (151:6.1–6.8); Veronica, Jairus’s daughter, and the weary Master (152:0.1–1.3); the three days of the gathering crowd, the king plot, the apostles for and against, the five loaves and two fishes, and the twelve baskets (152:2.1–2.10); the cry to make him king, his refusal, the words of the lad Mark, and the charge to pray for Peter (152:3.1–3.3); the night of contrary wind and Peter’s dream (152:4.1–4.4); Jesus on the stone by the shore and the rebuke that followed (152:5.1–5.5); and the rest at Gennesaret, the journey to Jerusalem, and the return to Bethsaida (152:6.1–7.3).
ch09.b065: Character details come from Paper 139: Andrew’s reluctance to praise and his freedom from jealousy of his brother (139:1.6, 139:1.10); Peter’s swings of feeling (139:2.3, 139:2.8); Philip’s stewardship, his wish to be shown, and his admiration of the Master’s generosity (139:5.2–5.7); Simon Zelotes’s Zealot temper and his admiration of the Master’s calm (139:11.1–11.5); and the twins’ handling of the crowds (139:9.3).
ch09.b066: Added fiction includes the characters’ inner thoughts and feelings (the words Andrew could not say to his brother, Philip’s tears when he stopped counting as he passed the bread, Simon Zelotes’s raised fist, the look on Judas’s face); sensory detail of the squall, the twilight, and the sea at night; Nathaniel’s joke about the birds; the twins seating the crowd; Philip handing a fish to a child; the words exchanged by Philip, Matthew, and Judas over their sums; the evening Andrew mended a net with his brother; and Andrew sitting beside the Master on the shore. The contents of Philip’s bag and the order in which Peter was seized in the water are invented; the text says only that Andrew, James, and John pulled him out.
ch09.b067: The words of Jesus are retold, not quoted, following the sense of the text.
